items.stem: What is meant by the amplitude of an oscillation?
options: the distance travelled in one oscillation
the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position
items.answer: the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position
items.markingKey: Amplitude x₀ is the maximum displacement.

items.stem: Distinguish between displacement and amplitude for an oscillating object.
items.answer: Displacement is the distance (with direction) from the equilibrium position at any instant and varies with time; amplitude is the maximum displacement and is constant for an undamped oscillation.
items.markingKey: displacement: instantaneous, from equilibrium, varies [1]; amplitude: maximum displacement [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by phase difference between two oscillations of the same frequency.
items.answer: It is the fraction of a cycle by which one oscillation leads or lags the other, expressed as an angle (2π × fraction of a period).
items.markingKey: fraction of cycle between them [1]; expressed as angle in rad/degrees [1] [2]

items.stem: A mass on a vertical spring completes 20 oscillations in 4.0 s with an amplitude of 0.010 m. Calculate the angular frequency.
items.answer: 31.4 rad s⁻¹
items.markingKey: T = 4.0/20 = 0.20 s; ω = 2π/T = 31.4 rad s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A car body on its suspension completes 20 oscillations in 16 s with an amplitude of 0.060 m. Calculate the period, the frequency and the angular frequency.

A simple pendulum oscillates with a period of 2.0 s and an amplitude of 0.020 m. (a) Define frequency. (b) Calculate the frequency. (c) State the total distance moved in one complete oscillation. (d) A second identical oscillator lags by 0.50 s. State the phase difference.
items.answer: (a) Number of oscillations per unit time. (b) 0.50 Hz (c) 0.080 m (d) π/2 rad (90°)
items.markingKey: (a) Number of oscillations per unit time [1] (b) f = 1/T: 0.50 Hz [1] (c) 4x₀: 0.080 m [1] (d) π/2 rad (90°) [1]

items.stem: An oscillator has a frequency of 50 Hz. What is its angular frequency?
items.answer: 314 rad s⁻¹

items.stem: Explain why angular frequency, rather than frequency, is used in the equations of simple harmonic motion.
items.answer: SHM is related to motion in a circle: the displacement x = x₀ sin ωt uses an angle ωt in radians, which increases by 2π each period; ω = 2πf makes the equations simpler.
items.markingKey: link to circular motion / angle ωt [1]; 2π per cycle, ω = 2πf [1] [2]

items.stem: A student says that two oscillators with different frequencies have a constant phase difference. Explain why this is incorrect.
items.answer: If frequencies differ, one completes cycles faster, so the phase difference between them changes continuously with time; a constant phase difference requires equal frequencies.
items.markingKey: phase difference changes with time [1]; constant only for same frequency [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain what is meant by phase difference between two oscillations of the same frequency. (b) A student says that two oscillators with different frequencies have a constant phase difference. Explain why this is incorrect.
items.answer: (a) It is the fraction of a cycle by which one oscillation leads or lags the other, expressed as an angle (2π × fraction of a period). (b) If frequencies differ, one completes cycles faster, so the phase difference between them changes continuously with time; a constant phase difference requires equal frequencies.
items.markingKey: (a) fraction of cycle between them [1]; expressed as angle in rad/degrees [1] [2] (b) phase difference changes with time [1]; constant only for same frequency [1] [2]

items.stem: Tariq watches two pendulums of period 1.2 s. Pendulum P passes through its equilibrium position moving to the right 0.400 s before pendulum Q does the same. Calculate the phase difference between P and Q, in radians and in degrees.
items.markingKey: fraction of cycle = Δt/T = 0.333 [1]; φ = 2π × fraction = 2.09 rad = 120° [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya watches two pendulums of period 2.0 s. Pendulum P passes through its equilibrium position moving to the right 1.33 s before pendulum Q does the same. Calculate the phase difference between P and Q, in radians and in degrees. State which oscillation leads.
items.answer: 4.19 rad (240°); P leads
items.markingKey: fraction of cycle = Δt/T = 0.667 [1]; φ = 2π × fraction = 4.19 rad = 240° [1]; P leads [1] [3]

items.stem: A tuning-fork prong oscillates with a period of 0.00455 s and an amplitude of 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m. (a) Define frequency. (b) Calculate the frequency. (c) State the total distance moved in one complete oscillation. (d) A second identical oscillator lags by 0.00114 s. State the phase difference.
items.answer: (a) Number of oscillations per unit time. (b) 220 Hz (c) 0.0020 m (d) π/2 rad (90°)
items.markingKey: (a) Number of oscillations per unit time [1] (b) f = 1/T: 220 Hz [1] (c) 4x₀: 0.0020 m [1] (d) π/2 rad (90°) [1]

items.stem: A simple pendulum oscillates with a period of 1.8 s and an amplitude of 0.040 m. (a) Define frequency. (b) Calculate the frequency. (c) Calculate the angular frequency. (d) A second identical oscillator lags by 0.45 s. State the phase difference.
items.answer: (a) Number of oscillations per unit time. (b) 0.556 Hz (c) 3.49 rad s⁻¹ (d) π/2 rad (90°)
items.markingKey: (a) Number of oscillations per unit time [1] (b) f = 1/T: 0.556 Hz [1] (c) ω = 2π/T (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.49 rad s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (d) π/2 rad (90°) [1]

items.stem: Which equation defines simple harmonic motion?
items.answer: a = −ω²x
items.markingKey: Acceleration proportional to displacement and directed towards the equilibrium position.

items.stem: Explain the significance of the minus sign in a = −ω²x.
items.answer: The acceleration is always in the opposite direction to the displacement, i.e. always directed towards the equilibrium position (restoring).
items.markingKey: acceleration opposite to displacement [1]; towards equilibrium [1] [2]

items.stem: State the conditions for an oscillation to be simple harmonic.
items.answer: The acceleration (or restoring force) is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and always directed towards that point.
items.markingKey: a ∝ x [1]; directed towards equilibrium (opposite to x) [1] [2]

items.stem: A tuning-fork prong performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ m and period 0.00455 s. Calculate the maximum acceleration.
items.answer: 953 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: a₀ = ω²x₀ = (2π/0.00455)² × 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 953 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A tuning-fork prong performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 0.0010 m and period 0.00227 s. Calculate the maximum speed and the maximum acceleration.
items.answer: v₀ = 2.77 m s⁻¹; a₀ = 7660 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: ω = 2π/T = 2770 rad s⁻¹ [1]; v₀ = ωx₀ = 2.77 m s⁻¹ [1]; a₀ = ω²x₀ = 7660 m s⁻² [1] [3]

items.stem: A molecule in a crystal lattice (modelled classically) performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 2.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m and period 1.00 × 10⁻¹³ s. (a) Calculate the angular frequency. (b) Calculate the speed when the displacement is 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m. (c) Calculate the acceleration at this displacement and state its direction.
items.answer: (a) 6.28 × 10¹³ rad s⁻¹ (b) 1090 m s⁻¹ (c) 3.95 × 10¹⁶ m s⁻², towards the equilibrium position
items.markingKey: (a) ω = 2π/T = 6.28 × 10¹³ rad s⁻¹ [1] (b) v = ω√(x₀² − x²) [1]; = 1090 m s⁻¹ [1] (c) a = ω²x = 3.95 × 10¹⁶ m s⁻² [1]; towards equilibrium [1] [5]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 0.20 kg on a horizontal track is attached between two springs. When displaced by x, the resultant force on it is −20x (in N, with x in m). It is displaced by 0.040 m and released. (a) Calculate the period. (b) Calculate the maximum speed. (c) State the displacement–time equation for the trolley, taking t = 0 at release.
items.markingKey: (a) T = 2π/ω: 0.628 s [1] (b) v₀ = ωx₀ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.40 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (c) x = 0.040 cos(10t) [1]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 0.50 kg on a horizontal track is attached between two springs. When displaced by x, the resultant force on it is −80x (in N, with x in m). It is displaced by 0.050 m and released. (a) Show that the trolley performs simple harmonic motion. (b) Calculate the maximum speed. (c) Calculate the maximum acceleration.
items.answer: (a) a = F/m = −(80/0.50)x, so a ∝ −x: SHM with ω² = k/m. (b) 0.632 m s⁻¹ (c) 8.00 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) a = −(k/m)x [1]; a ∝ −x so SHM [1] [2] (b) v₀ = ωx₀ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.632 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (c) a₀ = ω²x₀: 8.00 m s⁻² [1]

items.stem: In SHM, where is the speed of the oscillator a maximum?
options: it is the same at all points
halfway between equilibrium and maximum displacement
items.answer: at the equilibrium position
items.markingKey: v = ω√(x₀² − x²) is greatest at x = 0.

items.stem: In SHM, where is the magnitude of the acceleration a maximum?
items.answer: at maximum displacement
items.markingKey: |a| = ω²|x|.

items.stem: Explain why the period of a simple harmonic oscillator does not depend on its amplitude.
items.answer: a = −ω²x: a larger amplitude gives proportionally larger accelerations and speeds, so the object covers the larger distance in the same time; T = 2π/ω depends only on ω.
items.markingKey: acceleration scales with displacement [1]; T = 2π/ω independent of x₀ [1] [2]

items.stem: Show that x = x₀ sin ωt satisfies a = −ω²x.
items.answer: v = dx/dt = x₀ω cos ωt; a = dv/dt = −x₀ω² sin ωt = −ω²x.
items.markingKey: differentiate once correctly [1]; second derivative = −ω²x [1] [2]

items.stem: A student claims a ball bouncing vertically on a hard floor performs SHM. Explain why this is incorrect.
items.answer: While in the air its acceleration is constant (g downwards), not proportional to displacement from a fixed point, so it does not satisfy a = −ω²x.
items.markingKey: acceleration constant (g) [1]; not ∝ displacement [1] [2]

items.markingKey: ω = 2πf = 7.85 rad s⁻¹ [1]; x = x₀ sin ωt with calculator in radians [1]; = 0.0115 m [1] [3]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 0.50 kg on a horizontal track is attached between two springs. When displaced by x, the resultant force on it is −20x (in N, with x in m). It is displaced by 0.030 m and released. (a) Show that the trolley performs simple harmonic motion. (b) Calculate the period.
items.answer: (a) a = F/m = −(20/0.50)x, so a ∝ −x: SHM with ω² = k/m. (b) 0.993 s

items.stem: A trolley of mass 0.50 kg on a horizontal track is attached between two springs. When displaced by x, the resultant force on it is −20x (in N, with x in m). It is displaced by 0.050 m and released. (a) Calculate the angular frequency. (b) Calculate the period.
items.markingKey: (a) ω = √(k/m) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6.32 rad s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) T = 2π/ω: 0.993 s [1]

items.stem: For an undamped simple harmonic oscillator, which quantity remains constant?
items.answer: the total energy
items.markingKey: KE and PE interchange; total is constant.

items.stem: Describe the energy changes during one complete oscillation of a simple pendulum.
items.answer: At maximum displacement the energy is all gravitational PE; as the bob swings to the centre PE is converted to KE (maximum at the centre); then KE back to PE on the other side, and the sequence repeats; total energy constant if undamped.
items.markingKey: PE max at extremes, KE max at centre [1]; continuous interchange, total constant [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the graph of kinetic energy against displacement for SHM is an inverted parabola.
items.answer: Ek = ½mω²(x₀² − x²): a quadratic in x with a negative x² term, maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±x₀.
items.markingKey: Ek = ½mω²(x₀² − x²) [1]; quadratic, max at 0, zero at ±x₀ [1] [2]

items.stem: A pendulum bob of mass 0.050 kg performs SHM with period 1.2 s and amplitude 0.030 m. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation.
items.markingKey: E = ½mω²x₀² = ½ × 0.050 × (2π/1.2)² × 0.030² = 6.17 × 10⁻⁴ J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A pendulum bob of mass 0.10 kg performs SHM with period 0.50 s and amplitude 0.050 m. Calculate the kinetic energy and the potential energy when the displacement is 0.0375 m.

A mass of 0.50 kg on a spring oscillates with SHM at 2.0 Hz with amplitude 0.040 m. Damping is negligible. (a) Calculate the displacement at which the kinetic energy equals the potential energy. (b) Describe how the kinetic energy varies with displacement.
items.answer: (a) 0.0283 m (b) Maximum at x = 0, falling to zero at ±x₀ along an inverted parabola, Ek = ½mω²(x₀² − x²).
items.markingKey: (a) x = x₀/√2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.0283 m with unit [1] [2] (b) max at 0, zero at ±x₀ [1]; parabolic shape [1] [2]

items.stem: The total energy of a simple harmonic oscillator of mass m, angular frequency ω and amplitude x₀ is …
items.answer: ½mω²x₀²
items.markingKey: E = ½mv₀² with v₀ = ωx₀.

items.stem: Explain why, in a real oscillator, the total energy decreases with time.
items.answer: Resistive forces (air resistance, friction) do work against the motion, transferring energy to thermal energy of the surroundings; the amplitude decreases (damping).
items.markingKey: resistive forces do work [1]; energy dissipated as thermal energy, amplitude falls [1] [2]

items.stem: Show that the maximum kinetic energy of a simple harmonic oscillator is ½mω²x₀².
items.answer: Maximum speed v₀ = ωx₀, so Ek(max) = ½mv₀² = ½mω²x₀².
items.markingKey: v₀ = ωx₀ [1]; substitute into ½mv² [1] [2]

items.stem: A mass of 0.30 kg on a spring oscillates with SHM at 2.5 Hz with amplitude 0.050 m. Damping is negligible. (a) Calculate the maximum speed. (b) Calculate the displacement at which the kinetic energy equals the potential energy. (c) State the frequency at which the kinetic energy varies.

items.stem: What is meant by damping of an oscillation?
options: the transfer of energy to the oscillator by a driver
the oscillation of a system at its natural frequency
an increase in frequency due to an external force
the loss of energy and reduction of amplitude due to resistive forces
items.answer: the loss of energy and reduction of amplitude due to resistive forces
items.markingKey: Resistive forces remove energy from the oscillator.

items.stem: Distinguish between light damping, critical damping and heavy damping.
items.answer: Light: oscillates with amplitude decreasing gradually. Critical: returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without oscillating. Heavy: returns very slowly without oscillating.
items.markingKey: light correct [1]; critical and heavy distinguished [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how resonance can cause damage to a bridge and how engineers reduce the risk.
items.answer: If periodic forces (wind vortices, marching) have a frequency equal to the natural frequency, energy is transferred efficiently and the amplitude becomes very large, causing damage. Engineers add damping (dampers) or change the natural frequency (stiffness).
items.markingKey: driving frequency = natural frequency, large amplitude [1]; damping or change natural frequency [1] [2]

items.stem: Zara records the amplitude of a lightly damped pendulum. The amplitude falls by the same fraction every cycle: it is 10 cm initially and 9.0 cm after one cycle. Calculate the amplitude after 5 cycles.
items.markingKey: ratio = 0.90 per cycle; A = 10 × 0.90^5 = 5.90 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Chloe records the amplitude of a lightly damped pendulum. The amplitude falls by the same fraction every cycle: it is 10 cm initially and 8.5 cm after one cycle. Calculate the amplitude after 4 cycles and the fraction of the original energy remaining.

A vibration-testing rig in Singapore drives a metal strip with a natural frequency of 5.0 Hz. (a) State what is meant by resonance. (b) Calculate the period of a driving force that would cause resonance. (c) Suggest one way engineers could reduce the risk of damage from resonance.
items.answer: (a) Maximum amplitude of forced oscillations when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency. (b) 0.20 s (c) Fit dampers to increase damping, or change the stiffness/mass to move the natural frequency away from likely driving frequencies.
items.markingKey: (a) max amplitude [1]; driving = natural frequency [1] [2] (b) T = 1/f₀: 0.20 s [1] (c) Fit dampers to increase damping, or change the stiffness/mass to move the natural frequency away from likely driving frequencies [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State what is meant by the natural frequency of a system. (b) What is meant by damping of an oscillation?
items.answer: (a) The frequency at which it oscillates freely after being displaced (no driving force). (b) the loss of energy and reduction of amplitude due to resistive forces
items.markingKey: (a) free oscillation frequency [1] (b) Resistive forces remove energy from the oscillator.

items.stem: Explain why, at resonance, the amplitude of a forced oscillator is limited by damping.
items.answer: At resonance energy is transferred most efficiently; the amplitude rises until the energy lost per cycle to damping equals the energy supplied per cycle, so more damping gives a smaller maximum amplitude.
items.markingKey: maximum energy transfer at resonance [1]; energy loss balances input [1] [2]

items.stem: A trolley of mass 0.20 kg on a horizontal track is attached between two springs. When displaced by x, the resultant force on it is −20x (in N, with x in m). It is displaced by 0.050 m and released. (a) Show that the trolley performs simple harmonic motion. (b) Calculate the period. (c) Calculate the maximum acceleration.
items.answer: (a) a = F/m = −(20/0.20)x, so a ∝ −x: SHM with ω² = k/m. (b) 0.628 s (c) 5.0 m s⁻²

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The total energy of a simple harmonic oscillator of mass m, angular frequency ω and amplitude x₀ is … (b) State an expression for the kinetic energy of an oscillator in SHM at displacement x.
items.answer: (a) ½mω²x₀² (b) Ek = ½mω²(x₀² − x²)
items.markingKey: (a) E = ½mv₀² with v₀ = ωx₀. (b) correct expression [1]

items.stem: An undamped oscillator is modelled in a computer simulation. The mass is tripled while the amplitude and frequency stay the same. Predict, with a reason, how the total energy of the oscillation changes.
items.answer: The total energy of the oscillation triples.
items.markingKey: Using E = ½mω²x₀²: total energy of the oscillation ∝ mass; factor = 3.00 = 3.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A trolley between springs of mass 0.40 kg performs SHM with period 0.80 s and amplitude 0.040 m. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation.
items.markingKey: E = ½mω²x₀² = ½ × 0.40 × (2π/0.80)² × 0.040² = 0.0197 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A mass on a spring of mass 0.40 kg performs SHM with period 0.50 s and amplitude 0.020 m. Calculate the kinetic energy and the potential energy when the displacement is 0.012 m.

A mass of 0.15 kg on a spring oscillates with SHM at 1.5 Hz with amplitude 0.040 m. Damping is negligible. (a) Calculate the total energy of the oscillations. (b) Calculate the displacement at which the kinetic energy equals the potential energy. (c) Describe how the kinetic energy varies with displacement.
items.answer: (a) 0.0107 J (b) 0.0283 m (c) Maximum at x = 0, falling to zero at ±x₀ along an inverted parabola, Ek = ½mω²(x₀² − x²).
items.markingKey: (a) E = ½mv₀² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.0107 J with unit [1] [2] (b) x = x₀/√2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.0283 m with unit [1] [2] (c) max at 0, zero at ±x₀ [1]; parabolic shape [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how the amplitude of a lightly damped forced oscillator varies as the driving frequency is increased from zero to well above the natural frequency.
items.answer: Amplitude starts small (about the driver amplitude), rises to a sharp maximum at (just below) the natural frequency, then falls towards zero at high frequencies.
items.markingKey: rises to peak at natural frequency [1]; falls at higher frequency [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why soldiers are ordered to break step when crossing a bridge.
items.answer: Marching in step applies a periodic force; if its frequency matches a natural frequency of the bridge, resonance gives large-amplitude oscillations that could damage it.
items.markingKey: periodic force at a frequency [1]; resonance, large amplitude [1] [2]

items.stem: Aisha records the amplitude of a lightly damped pendulum. The amplitude falls by the same fraction every cycle: it is 12 cm initially and 9.60 cm after one cycle. Calculate the amplitude after 4 cycles.
items.markingKey: ratio = 0.80 per cycle; A = 12 × 0.80^4 = 4.92 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A vibration-testing rig in Lisbon drives a metal strip with a natural frequency of 8.0 Hz. (a) State what is meant by resonance. (b) Calculate the period of a driving force that would cause resonance. (c) Suggest one way engineers could reduce the risk of damage from resonance.
items.answer: (a) Maximum amplitude of forced oscillations when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency. (b) 0.125 s (c) Fit dampers to increase damping, or change the stiffness/mass to move the natural frequency away from likely driving frequencies.
items.markingKey: (a) max amplitude [1]; driving = natural frequency [1] [2] (b) T = 1/f₀: 0.125 s [1] (c) Fit dampers to increase damping, or change the stiffness/mass to move the natural frequency away from likely driving frequencies [1]

items.stem: Two identical pendulums oscillate with the same period T. One reaches its maximum displacement T/4 after the other. What is the phase difference?
items.answer: π/2 rad
items.markingKey: φ = 2πΔt/T = 2π/4.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student says that two oscillators with different frequencies have a constant phase difference. Explain why this is incorrect. (b) Explain why angular frequency, rather than frequency, is used in the equations of simple harmonic motion.
items.answer: (a) If frequencies differ, one completes cycles faster, so the phase difference between them changes continuously with time; a constant phase difference requires equal frequencies. (b) SHM is related to motion in a circle: the displacement x = x₀ sin ωt uses an angle ωt in radians, which increases by 2π each period; ω = 2πf makes the equations simpler.
items.markingKey: (a) phase difference changes with time [1]; constant only for same frequency [1] [2] (b) link to circular motion / angle ωt [1]; 2π per cycle, ω = 2πf [1] [2]

items.stem: Lucas watches two pendulums of period 1.2 s. Pendulum P passes through its equilibrium position moving to the right 0.800 s before pendulum Q does the same. Calculate the phase difference between P and Q, in radians and in degrees.
items.markingKey: fraction of cycle = Δt/T = 0.667 [1]; φ = 2π × fraction = 4.19 rad = 240° [1] [2]

items.stem: Leila watches two pendulums of period 0.40 s. Pendulum P passes through its equilibrium position moving to the right 0.267 s before pendulum Q does the same. Calculate the phase difference between P and Q, in radians and in degrees. State which oscillation leads.
items.answer: 4.19 rad (240°); P leads
items.markingKey: fraction of cycle = Δt/T = 0.667 [1]; φ = 2π × fraction = 4.19 rad = 240° [1]; P leads [1] [3]

items.stem: A trolley tethered between two springs oscillates with a period of 1.2 s and an amplitude of 0.060 m. (a) Define frequency. (b) Calculate the angular frequency. (c) A second identical oscillator lags by 0.30 s. State the phase difference. (d) Explain why the displacement is zero twice in each cycle.
items.answer: (a) Number of oscillations per unit time. (b) 5.24 rad s⁻¹ (c) π/2 rad (90°) (d) The object passes through the equilibrium position twice per cycle, once in each direction.
items.markingKey: (a) Number of oscillations per unit time [1] (b) ω = 2π/T (method/substitution) [1]; answer 5.24 rad s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (c) π/2 rad (90°) [1] (d) The object passes through the equilibrium position twice per cycle, once in each direction [1]

items.stem: A graph of acceleration a against displacement x for SHM is …
options: a straight line through the origin with a negative gradient
a straight line through the origin with a positive gradient
items.answer: a straight line through the origin with a negative gradient
items.markingKey: a = −ω²x: gradient −ω².

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Show that x = x₀ sin ωt satisfies a = −ω²x. (b) State the conditions for an oscillation to be simple harmonic.
items.answer: (a) v = dx/dt = x₀ω cos ωt; a = dv/dt = −x₀ω² sin ωt = −ω²x. (b) The acceleration (or restoring force) is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and always directed towards that point.
items.markingKey: (a) differentiate once correctly [1]; second derivative = −ω²x [1] [2] (b) a ∝ x [1]; directed towards equilibrium (opposite to x) [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain the significance of the minus sign in a = −ω²x. (b) Explain why the period of a simple harmonic oscillator does not depend on its amplitude.
items.answer: (a) The acceleration is always in the opposite direction to the displacement, i.e. always directed towards the equilibrium position (restoring). (b) a = −ω²x: a larger amplitude gives proportionally larger accelerations and speeds, so the object covers the larger distance in the same time; T = 2π/ω depends only on ω.
items.markingKey: (a) acceleration opposite to displacement [1]; towards equilibrium [1] [2] (b) acceleration scales with displacement [1]; T = 2π/ω independent of x₀ [1] [2]

items.stem: A car body on its suspension performs simple harmonic motion with amplitude 0.020 m and period 0.80 s. Calculate the maximum acceleration.
items.markingKey: a₀ = ω²x₀ = (2π/0.80)² × 0.020 = 1.23 m s⁻². (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: For small oscillations a simple pendulum of length l performs SHM with ω² = g/l. A pendulum of length 0.25 m is displaced by 0.050 m and released. Calculate the period and the maximum speed of the bob.

A trolley of mass 0.40 kg on a horizontal track is attached between two springs. When displaced by x, the resultant force on it is −40x (in N, with x in m). It is displaced by 0.030 m and released. (a) Show that the trolley performs simple harmonic motion. (b) Calculate the period. (c) Calculate the maximum acceleration.
items.answer: (a) a = F/m = −(40/0.40)x, so a ∝ −x: SHM with ω² = k/m. (b) 0.628 s (c) 3.0 m s⁻²

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) At what displacement is the kinetic energy of an oscillator in SHM equal to its potential energy? (b) The kinetic energy of an oscillator varies with time with a frequency that is …
items.answer: (a) x₀/√2 (b) twice the frequency of the oscillation
items.markingKey: (a) ½mω²(x₀² − x²) = ½mω²x² ⇒ x² = x₀²/2. (b) KE peaks twice per cycle.

items.stem: A mass–spring system oscillates with simple harmonic motion. The frequency is increased by 50% while the amplitude and mass stay the same. Predict, with a reason, how the total energy of the oscillation changes.
items.answer: The total energy of the oscillation becomes 2.25 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using E = ½mω²x₀²: total energy of the oscillation ∝ frequency^2.00; factor = 1.50^2.00 = 2.25. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A vibrating platform of mass 0.25 kg performs SHM with period 0.40 s and amplitude 0.050 m. Calculate the total energy of the oscillation.
items.markingKey: E = ½mω²x₀² = ½ × 0.25 × (2π/0.40)² × 0.050² = 0.0771 J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A trolley between springs of mass 0.050 kg performs SHM with period 1.0 s and amplitude 0.040 m. Calculate the kinetic energy and the potential energy when the displacement is 0.030 m.

A mass of 0.50 kg on a spring oscillates with SHM at 1.5 Hz with amplitude 0.040 m. Damping is negligible. (a) Calculate the maximum speed. (b) Calculate the total energy of the oscillations. (c) Calculate the displacement at which the kinetic energy equals the potential energy.
items.markingKey: (a) v₀ = 2πf x₀ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.377 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) E = ½mv₀² (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.0355 J with unit [1] [2] (c) x = x₀/√2 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 0.0283 m with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain how resonance can cause damage to a bridge and how engineers reduce the risk. (b) Explain why, at resonance, the amplitude of a forced oscillator is limited by damping.
items.answer: (a) If periodic forces (wind vortices, marching) have a frequency equal to the natural frequency, energy is transferred efficiently and the amplitude becomes very large, causing damage. Engineers add damping (dampers) or change the natural frequency (stiffness). (b) At resonance energy is transferred most efficiently; the amplitude rises until the energy lost per cycle to damping equals the energy supplied per cycle, so more damping gives a smaller maximum amplitude.
items.markingKey: (a) driving frequency = natural frequency, large amplitude [1]; damping or change natural frequency [1] [2] (b) maximum energy transfer at resonance [1]; energy loss balances input [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a child on a swing goes higher when pushed once per swing at the right moment.
items.answer: The pushes are at the natural frequency of the swing (resonance), so energy is added efficiently each cycle and the amplitude grows.
items.markingKey: identifies resonance or damping correctly [1]; links frequency/energy transfer to the effect [1]; uses terms natural and driving frequency correctly [1] [3]

items.stem: Sipho records the amplitude of a lightly damped pendulum. The amplitude falls by the same fraction every cycle: it is 12 cm initially and 10.2 cm after one cycle. Calculate the amplitude after 5 cycles.
items.markingKey: ratio = 0.85 per cycle; A = 12 × 0.85^5 = 5.32 cm. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A vibration-testing rig in Hanoi drives a metal strip with a natural frequency of 5.0 Hz. (a) Sketch-describe a graph of amplitude against driving frequency for light damping. (b) Describe the effect of increasing the damping on the graph.
items.answer: (a) Low at low frequency, sharp peak at about 5.0 Hz, falling towards zero at high frequency. (b) Peak amplitude lower, peak broader and slightly shifted to lower frequency.
items.markingKey: (a) peak at f₀ [1]; correct shape either side [1] [2] (b) lower [1]; broader / shift [1] [2]
